highlights.text: "spreading out" and "extension."
al-ṭaḥw means "spreading," a near-synonym of al-daḥw
glossing ṭaḥāhā as "He spread it" (basaṭahā)
highlights.note: Q 91:6 explained by its ordinary meaning

highlights.text: Illustrated with a line of poetry by ʿAlqama: a heart carried away by longing for beautiful women even as old age and gray hair were setting in.
two distinct sound roots: (1) fright/alarm, and (2) coming to someone's aid
faziʿa / yafzaʿu / fazaʿan — "to be frightened"
fazzaʿtu ʿanhu, reverses the sense: to remove the fright from someone
Poetic witness: "Tall, his gaze raised high … toward the dog's place of refuge."
a saying attributed to the Prophet, addressed to the Anṣār: "You are many at the call for aid, and few when there is gain to covet."
highlights.note: a saying attributed to the Prophet

highlights.text: the root points to "breaking and falling."
halāk — a falling/collapse, hence "destruction, perishing."
In al-Ḥuṭayʾa's line, mustahlik (of one pressing on to the watering-place) was glossed by some as "earnest, diligent" (jādd)
j-th indicates the gathering together of a thing
pulled out with all its roots and rootlets, so that nothing of it is left
a verse by al-Hudhalī: "The ropes did not stop until they had set him down beside the swarm, clearing away its jathth and smoking it out."
"to pierce / cut through a thing" (خرق)
"the exchange / returning of speech," i.e. answering
كلّمه فأجابه جوابًا = "he spoke to him and he answered him"
جُبْتُ الأرضَ = "I cut across the land"
أساء سمعًا فأساء جابةً — "he heard wrong, so he answered wrong"
the fitting-together of two things and the setting of them right
النُّصْح and النَّصِيحَة, meaning sincere advice or good faith
التَّوْبَةُ النَّصُوح ("sincere repentance")
نَاصِحُ الْجَيْب ("sincere of bosom") is used proverbially of someone pure in deed
one sound root whose core idea is a thing being drawn out and slipping away
نَسْل (nasl) is a child or progeny, so named because it is drawn out from its mother
Ibn Fāris cites Qur'an 21:96 — {وهم من كل حدب ينسلون}, "from every height they come hurrying."
to shake or jolt something violently, typically so as to dislodge, empty, or extract what it holds
God "nataqa" the mountain — He raised it up, shaking it, above them.
three linked ideas: giving light, turbulent motion, and instability
النُّور (light) and النَّار (fire) both belong here — named for their illumination, and because fire is restless and quick-moving
a line of Imruʾ al-Qays about sighting a distant fire
a single root whose core idea is throwing and flinging away
قَذَفَ / يَقْذِفُ / قَذْفًا — to throw or hurl something
He cites an unattributed line: "A missile of a driven-off shayṭān, which he hurled — and it became a growth in the jaw-glands of an aged she-camel,"
a single core meaning: entering or plunging into something abruptly, with roughness and rash boldness
qahama fi l-umuri (he plunged into affairs) means he threw himself into matters with no prior experience or training
one sound root whose core idea is trimming something even — paring it down and putting it right
The قَلَم (qalam, pen) belongs here, he reports, because it is named from the paring done to it, exactly as a nail is pared
He cites Q 3:44, "when they cast their aqlām,"
"one who follows another as a helper/supporter." Cited: "Send him with me as a *ridʾ* (helper) to confirm me" (Qur'an 28:34).
one consistent idea: uprooting, so that nothing is left
God wiped out the denier with a punishment
al-Farazdaq: "the biting of a time, O son of Marwān, that left of wealth nothing but what was swept away (musḥat) or pared down (mujallaf)."
الأَساطير (asāṭīr) — falsehoods, baseless tales
saṭr means a written line, and writing itself (khaṭṭ, kitāba)
one placed in authority over something to oversee it, tend its affairs, and record its work
A verse of Jarīr uses it of a line in a register
a single core idea: taking something off the surface of something else
because the ship "scrapes" the water, as though peeling it
an animal comes stealthily "its belly scraping the ground,"
a yearly raid that "chafes the hoof-heels as the safan chafes."
a single core notion: elevation or height
the Arabs call cloud samāʾ and rain samāʾ
its origin is simw, from the same root of elevation
the saying "We kept treading the samāʾ until we reached you,"
the three letters s-t-r point to one idea — covering
satartu al-shayʾa satran, "I covered the thing."
anything at all that you conceal or screen yourself with
setting a thing straight — correcting what is bent in it
ثَقِفْتُ بِهِ = "I got hold of him,"
"If you get hold of me, then kill me … but if I am [not] laid hold of, you shall yet see my mettle."
one root whose core sense is leaving off and letting be
وَدَعَهُ (wadaʿahu) = he left him/it
The common imperative دَعْ (daʿ, "leave it, let it be") belongs here.
"Would that I knew about my friend — what overcame him in love, until he left off (wadaʿah)."
اختصموا / تخاصموا = "they quarreled with one another"
خصم and خصيم both = "opponent"
Of an affair that keeps going wrong, the Arabs say: "no side of it is stopped up but another side opens"
two distinct and directly opposite roots
خَفِيَ الشَّيْءُ ("the thing became hidden"); أَخْفَيْتُهُ ("I hid it")
is read as meaning "I make it manifest / bring it out," rather than "I hide it."
the flood "drove them out from their burrows
leanness/hollowness and being sunken-in
al-makhmaṣa = hunger, famine — because a hungry person's belly is hollow/lean
Citation (al-A'shā): people feast through winter nights while their neighbor-women go hungry (khamā'iṣ) at night.
one basic idea: reaching the end of something
Placing a seal on something.
the last thing the drinkers find of it, as they drink, is the scent of musk
أَخَذْتِ خَاتَامِي بِغَيْرِ حَقٍّ — "You took my signet-ring without right."
he glosses the Prophet as خَاتَمُ الْأَنْبِيَاء, "the seal of the prophets," giving the reason as: because he is the last of them
highlights.note: Ibn Fāris's own gloss of Q 33:40

highlights.text: Al-zamharīr (الزَّمْهَرِيرُ) — intense, bitter cold
Illustrated with a verse of al-Aʿshā describing sheltered women who "have seen neither sun nor zamharīr" — i.e., never exposed to either scorching heat or bitter cold.
